column2: It is the temperature above which a distinct liquid phase cannot exist—the boundary where the liquid and gas phases become indistinguishable. Like melting point is not just "a temperature" but specifically the boundary realized by solid-liquid transition, critical temperature is not just "a temperature" but specifically the boundary where liquid and gas phases become identical (the endpoint of the liquid-gas coexistence curve). Unlike melting/boiling points which are transition boundaries (where a phase changes into another), the critical temperature is a limit boundary—the point where the distinction between phases ceases to exist. But this is still a legitimate "state of matter boundary" under PMDs definition. (a different kind of limit, not just a direction), so it has this potentinal to be a class.
column4: In thermodynamics, a critical point (or critical state) is the end point of a phase equilibrium curve.@en

column2: Dilatometric softening temperature” refers to a specific measured temperature value obtained under standardised test conditions (dilatometry). It is not a universal type of entity but rather a particular value of the quality temperature
column4: The temperature at which the length of a sample in a dilatometer, with considerable external force applied to the sample in the course of heating at constant rate, reaches a maximal value and begins to decrease with further increases in temperature. The appearance of the maximum on the dilatometric curve is connected with the parallel influence of sample dilatation with increasing temperature and sample deformation due to the viscous flow. The position of the maximum can correspond approximately to a certain viscosity of the studied glass. Usually this viscosity is assumed to be equal to 10^11 P. However this value depends a great deal on the external load applied to the sample (the greater the load the higher corresponding viscosity), on the area of sample section (the greater the area the lower viscosity), on the value of TEC for the studied substance in its liquid state (the higher TEC the lower viscosity), on the rate of heating and on the previous thermal history of the sample (the higher the heating rate the lower viscosity; the lower the fictive temperature of the substance the lower viscosity). Thus the actual  viscosity  values at dilatometric softening temperatures could differ from the value stated above as greatly as  one order of magnitude. See also deformation point. unit = °C, symbol = Mg@en
